notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0022.stoa045a.opp-l: The text is a heavily corrupted scan; evident readings have been translated (e.g. 'sauciam' read as 'sanctam', 'vetere laudem' as 'vetere tandem', 'formam' as 'farinam', 'meus bona' as 'mens bona'). Several biblical references printed in the edition are garbled (e.g. 'I Cor. VI' for 1 Cor. 7:15, 'Jerem. XI, 10' for 11:19, 'Esai. IX, 40' for 9:10); corrected forms are given. 'Patri placentem' (pleasing to the Father) differs from the usual 'Deo placentem' of Rom. 12:1 but is translated as printed. The final words of the Isaiah quotation ('and they received gold') are taken as the author's, not the prophet's.

Line 3: 'aed ingemiscat habitationem quoe de cælo est' read as 'sed ingemiscat habitationem quae de caelo est' (echoing 2 Cor. 5:2); the clause seems truncated. The closing 'In disciplina perseverate, filii' (Heb. 12:7) appears to run straight into the next sentence; 'filii' may belong to a lost continuation. The sentence 'Quod sicut ille qui alio tendit...' is syntactically broken in the Latin. Line 6: the reference 'Apoc. xx, 9' for 'there is nothing on earth like him' is wrong; the words are from Job 41:24 (Vulgate). 'Hebr. XXII, 8' is evidently Heb. 12:8. Line 5: the Numbers reference is to 33:7 and the Exodus quotation is 14:5–6; printed references are garbled. Os Eroth is kept as the name the commentary interprets ('mouth of the nobles').

Line 9: the text is broken. After 'five mon-' (presumably 'months') the edition jumps without transition into the middle of another discussion; the account of the rest of station 8 and of stations 9–12 is missing, and the passage resumes with a quotation ('...in my members, fighting against the law of my mind') which is Rom. 7:23, though the edition cites 2 Cor. 11:2. Line 7: 'victoria; palmarum' read as 'victoriarum palmarum' (palms of victory). Line 10: the citation 'Exod. 11:22' is given as printed; the passage is Num. 11:17. 'Graves of Craving' renders Sepulcra concupiscentiae (Hebrew Kibroth-hattaavah). Line 11: 'Quo perfidiae impura livore' is awkward; translated as it stands.

Station names are given in their usual English forms (Rithmah, Rimmon-perez, Libnah, Rissah, Kehelathah, Shapher) for the text's Rethma, Remon-phares, Lebna, Ressa, Calatha, Arsaphar; the heading spells the first 'Rehtma'. 'Antmnsa' (line 17) is read as 'animosa', 'bold'. 'Exod. xi, 22' in the previous stretch should be Num. 11:17; similar reference slips in the printed edition (e.g. Hab. 3:2 for 3:3, Rom. 7:14 for 7:24) are kept or corrected only as evident.

Several references are misprinted or misassigned in the edition: 'Sufficientia nostra' is 2 Cor. 3:5-6; 'Statutum est hominibus semel mori' is Heb. 9:27; 'Quae vivit [in deliciis]' is 1 Tim. 5:6 ('vivetis' read as 'vivit'); Jer. 5:30; Luke 9:43. In the Hashmonah section the text says Elisha enjoined Gehazi, which matches 2 Kgs 4:29 though the Latin order ('Elisaeum ... Giezi injunxisse') is inverted; translated by the biblical sense. 'Doctrix ... est Dei disciplina' paraphrases Wis. 8:4 but is attributed to Solomon; 'ejus custodia virga correctionis est' is obscure. 'non sequamur modo' read as 'let us not merely follow'.

Several biblical references in the edition are misprinted and have been silently corrected in the translation: Matt. 'x. 26' to 5:26; Exod. 'X, 20' to 20:20; Ps. 'IV, 5' to 41:5 (Vulgate); Ps. 'ex, 1' to 110:1 (Vulgate cx; the wording matches Ps. 110:1, 'confitebor... in concilio justorum'); Ps. 'XlVIII, 8' to 28:8 (Vulgate). 'Eccles.' and 'Eccl.' references are to Sirach (Ecclesiasticus). 'quia consilium bonum custodiet te...' echoes Prov. 2:11. In line 26 'relaxaremur' shifts from the soul to 'we'; kept as in the text. 'punor' read as 'purior'. 'Sup. 1,3' read as Wis. 1:3.

Line 31: 'certiorem tamen eum facturos...' is compressed; rendered as the envoys assuring the king that Moses would not even ask for water free of charge. Line 33: the edition cites Eccl. 28 for the quotation from James 3; reference kept as printed. Line 34: 'Psal ac' read as Ps. 90; Oboth 'in magos' rendered 'against magicians'. Line 35: 'MUra' read as 'ultra' ('beyond'); 'tutam a, firmam' read as 'tutam ac firmam'; Gospel and Hebrews references corrected from scanning errors (Matt. 7:25, Heb. 11:13).

Line 38: the parenthesis opened at 'Unde subjungit' is never closed in the edition; 'Scoti' is evidently a misreading of 'Seon' (Sihon). Line 39: 'Deut. XXXIX' is a misprint (Deuteronomy has 34 chapters; the blessings and curses are in ch. 27-28, Moses' death in ch. 34); 'Bethsimon' and 'Belsachin' are taken as Beth-jeshimoth and Abel-shittim. The final sentence is grammatically loose in the Latin ('reponatur nobis' attached to the quotation); rendered by sense. Dibon-gad is glossed 'apiarium tentationum' (beehive of temptations), presumably a corruption of an etymology such as 'abundance of temptations'.

This stretch is not part of the treatise on the stations: it is the Maurist editors' preface to the Ambrosiaster commentaries on Paul, which follows in PL 17. 'Ante annum 584' is read as 384, the year of Damasus' death (scanning error). 'Beato DII'Has' is read as 'beato Damaso'. 'Patriciano' is taken as the Patricians, a heretical sect. 'In Epist. ad Timoth. cap. III' at the end presumably means 1 Timothy. Other obvious scanning errors (eat for est, aed for sed, Ii for si) are silently corrected.

This stretch is not the treatise on the 42 stations but part of the editors' (Maurist) preface on the Ambrosiaster commentaries on Paul. Scanning errors read as evident: 'ttt Hilarium tub' as 'ut Hilarium sub'; 'Nomine tenuI' as 'nomine tenus'; 'Ii post errore. Felicia' as 'si post errorem Felicis'; 'trit' as 'erit'. In line 52 'tum agnoverunt' is taken as '[editores] tum'; 'judicii trud 'toris' is corrupt, perhaps 'acrioris' or 'eruditioris', rendered 'sharper judgement'. 'In metendis' (line 49) is rendered 'gleaning'; the intended reading may be a word meaning 'excerpting'.

nodes.text: APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF SAINT AMBROSE.
Part one.
CONTAINING THE WORKS ADMITTED BY THE BENEDICTINES IN THEIR EDITION.
TREATISE ON THE FORTY-TWO STATIONS OF THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL.

1 The book of Numbers, of which we are now speaking, is one of the five books of Moses. We read that it is called by that name because, by God's command, it contains the number and count of the full-grown men of the Israelite people who came out of Egypt. For thus God spoke to Moses: Take the sum of the whole congregation of the children of Israel from twenty years old and upward, by the houses of their families, everyone going out to fight in Israel. So, since the Lord commanded that men from twenty years old and upward, and fit for battle, be numbered, it is plain that he meant full-grown men. From this sum are excluded women, because of the hindrance of female weakness; slaves, as degenerate in life and morals; and Egyptians, as foreigners and barbarians (Origen, Homily 1 on Numbers, in Rufinus' version). Only Israelites are numbered, and not all of them, but only those outstanding in strength and courage. For thus it is written: The numbering of the children of Israel with their army, from twenty years old and upward, everyone going out to fight in Israel, etc. (Num. 1:45). Nor is this without a mystery: for while a childish and unsteady mind, or a womanish and slack sloth, is in us, or while we bear Egyptian or barbarous manners, we do not deserve to be numbered in God's holy reckoning. Then in the same book the journeys, departures and stations of the children of Israel, from the borders of Egypt up to the time and place at which Moses died, are recounted by God's command. For it says: And Moses wrote down their departures and their stations, by the word of the Lord (ibid.). Nor indeed was Moses commanded by the Lord to write this without cause, for [it was] for our instruction; for the Apostle says: All these things happened to them in figure; and they were written for our correction (1 Cor. 10:11), so that, reading and proving how great dangers threaten us on this journey to the land of the living, how great the ambushes of enemies, the clashes of spiritual wars, the perils of seas and rivers, of the world and of pleasures (Origen, Homily 27 on Numbers, in Rufinus' version), we may not pursue our road sluggishly or slackly, lest, as the day slips away, we fail in the middle of the journey, overwhelmed by the darkness of night. For it is by night that the firstborn of Egypt are struck by the destroyer (Exod. 12:29); by night the soul of the greedy rich man is demanded back by demons (Luke 12:20). But girding ourselves prudently for the journey, and bravely prepared for wars, let us pass from virtue to virtue; and may the Lord our God go before us, before our face, defeating our enemies and carrying us as a mother [carries] her son, and leading us by day through the cloud and by night through fire, so that at last, having overcome every 2 difficulty of the road and the attacks of the adverse powers, we may complete our journey gloriously. Now the stations of the children of Israel are reckoned as forty-two in number, and by reason of the number they contain, of ten, of four and of two, they teach us many mysteries. Wishing to explain this to you, brothers, pay attention, I beg you, and fix [it] in your memory, so that you may not be found despisers of the word, and your soul may not become the path where the scattered seeds do not sprout: and, it says, the birds of the sky come and snatch them away. Take these things in, then, and store them in your hearts. The number ten is mystical, and not a little commended by Moses: for to it he refers firstfruits, offerings and vows. For he says: Every tithe of the land, and of the fruit of the trees, is the Lord's; and every tithe of oxen and sheep, and everything that comes into the count under the rod, the tenth shall be holy to the Lord (Lev. 27:30 ff.). Then Jacob, when God appeared to him on the road as he was setting out to his uncle Laban in Mesopotamia, promised, saying: Of all that you give me, I will give a tenth to you (Gen. 28:22). For this reason Noah, who was the first in the Old Scripture to be declared righteous, is presented as tenth from the first-formed man, not to show the age of those then living, or to prescribe the number of men, but so that it might be plainly taught that, just as ten is the most perfect of the numbers that follow unity, so tranquillity in the soul is truly the end of the actions of life. For three multiplied by itself makes up nine, and in the divine oracles signifies strife, discord and wars, as is evident in the four and five kings at odds and attacking one another. But unity, coming upon nine, completes ten, and signifies peace and friendship. For when nine kings were contending, wise Abraham, arriving as if a tenth, brought, with God's favour, calm in place of storm, peace in place of war, victory in place of death. Hence he also paid tithes to Melchizedek, priest of the most high God. The number ten, then, is perfect, and signifies unity. The number four too is itself mystical, and is commended in Scripture: for the prophetic word declares that the beautiful light, which shows itself and other things, and the begetters of light, the sun and the moon, and the brilliant choir of the stars, which by rising and setting mark the bounds of night and day, months and years, were created on the fourth day. The roots of the world are counted as four: earth, water, fire and air. 3 And the yearly changes of the seasons are as many: winter, summer, spring and autumn. Then, offerings to God from the fruits of the earth are forbidden before the fourth year. For thus it is written: The fruit of the land shall be unclean to you for three years; you shall not eat of it; but in the fourth year all its fruit shall be holy and praiseworthy to the Lord (Lev. 19:23-24). And rightly: for in four are contained all things, point, line, surface and solid, the measures of all things. In it also are the chief musical concords. Further, the sides of a square must be equal. And equality is the mother of justice, which is the leader and mistress of the other virtues. Four, then, intimates justice. Finally, two is not itself without a mystery. For we read that the widow who put two coins into the treasury is commended by the Lord with remarkable praise (Luke 21:2). The Samaritan paid out two coins for the care of the wounded man (Luke 10:35). Christ the Saviour spent two days among the Samaritans (John 4:43): for it signifies twofold charity, that is, of God and of neighbour: On these two, says the Lord, hangs the whole Law and the Prophets (Matt. 22:40). So the stations of the children of Israel from the borders of Egypt to the land of promise are recounted by Moses as forty-two. So too Saint Matthew, describing the generation of Christ, enumerates forty-two. For he says: from Abraham to David, fourteen generations; from David to the deportation to Babylon, fourteen generations; and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ, fourteen generations (Matt. 1:17): to show that the true Israelite, who hastens to come from the Egypt of this world to heaven, the true land of the living, through so many dangers and temptations of enemies, must be armed with peace through ten, justice through four, charity through two. With peace, because it is written: God has called us in peace (1 Cor. 7:15). With justice, because the same Apostle says: Stand, clothed with the breastplate of justice (Eph. 6:14). With charity, because charity covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4:8). So Christ to the Virgin, Israel to the Jordan, the Christian to heaven, come by an equal number of stations. But now let us consider the departures of Israel themselves one by one.

1st station, RAMESES. — The order of the departures and the distinction of the stations of the children of Israel going out of Egypt to the land promised to the fathers are very necessary to know for those who strive to walk after God and aspire to progress in the virtues, because of the mysteries contained in them (Origen, Homily 27, in Rufinus' version). For the things that were done bodily among the people of the fathers not only show us history and the sequence of events, but, understood spiritually, are of the greatest benefit for our instruction. This is what the Apostle had in view when he said in the letter to the Romans: Whatever things were written were written for our teaching (Rom. 15:4). And to Timothy: All Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, for reproving, for correcting and for instructing in justice, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work (2 Tim. 3:16-17). We read, then, that the children of Israel, after the whole of Egypt had been struck by so many plagues, at the time appointed by the heavenly oracle, in order to set out into the wilderness to sacrifice to the Lord God, leaving the land of Goshen, which they had received to dwell in, first assembled at the city of Rameses; there they halted, and there they made their first station. Rameses is a city of Egypt, fortified by the Hebrews when, as Pharaoh raged against them, they were oppressed with clay, bricks and straw. For thus it is written: And they built fortified cities for Pharaoh, Pithom, Rameses and On (Exod. 1:11). It is situated, moreover, at the farthest borders of that kingdom, as is found in the book of Exodus (Exod. 12:37). In this station the people of the fathers, having slain the lamb and smeared its blood on the thresholds and both doorposts of their houses, escaped the destroyer's blow; in this [station] Egypt saw its firstborn destroyed; in this the people, by the word of God, gathered for themselves unleavened flour, and vessels of silver and gold borrowed from the Egyptians. Each of the things that have been said, brothers, is full of mysteries, and profits our discipline. First, because Rameses, according to some, is interpreted 'turbulent commotion', which signifies penitence: for through it a turbulent commotion takes place in the sinner, so that the oldness of sin may be abolished and the newness of grace brought in; so that the old man may be fastened to the cross and the new man rise again; so that, the old way of life of the flesh being at last laid aside, the newness of the spirit may be brought in. Penitence, then, produces great commotion and disturbance. Therefore the prophet [says]: After I recognised [it], I groaned (Jer. 31). He, then, who desires to set out for the promised homeland of the eternal inheritance, and approaches to offer himself to the Lord God as a living sacrifice, holy, 4 pleasing to the Father, must first go to Rameses, that is, the commotion that comes about through penitence, and there fix his station. There Ahab fixed his station, when, having torn his garment and put on haircloth, he fasted, slept in sackcloth, and walked with bowed head (3 Kings 21:27). There the king of Nineveh fixed his station, when, rising from his throne, he took off his own robe and, clothed in sackcloth, sat in ashes (Jon. 3:6). There the Corinthians fixed their station, when they were made sorrowful according to God: a sorrow which, as the Apostle writes, works penitence unto lasting salvation (2 Cor. 7:10). Next, what else is the slaying of the lamb than the passion of Christ, who, as the Prophet says, was led like an innocent lamb to be sacrificed (Jer. 11:19)? By his blood poured on the posts of the houses we are freed from the Destroyer; because, through Christ's passion shared with us by the sacraments, we are freed from him who had the dominion of death, that is, the devil, as the Apostle writes to the Hebrews (Heb. 2:14). Therefore in another place he says: Christ, in order to sanctify the people by his own blood, suffered outside the gate (Heb. 13:12). In this station too the firstborn of Egypt are destroyed; that is, the depraved affections of the flesh, and the evil desires that war against the soul. And the Egyptians are destroyed when you do not do the works of darkness; the Egyptians are destroyed when you live not carnally but spiritually; the Egyptians are destroyed when you either drive impure and filthy thoughts from your heart or do not admit them at all. Therefore to the one asking: Who will free me from the body of this death? the Apostle answered: The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom. 7:24-25). In this station flour, silver and gold are heaped up. Flour, from which bread is made, is the teaching of Christ; for Christ is bread, as John says: I am the living bread (John 6:51). Silver signifies the divine word: For the words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire, proved in the earth, purified sevenfold (Ps. 11:7). Gold is a good mind, which is not undeservedly compared to gold: for as gold excels the other metals, so a good mind in man is superior to the other parts of human substance. Three things, then, are heaped up in Rameses, flour, silver and gold: teaching, the word and a good mind, in which the wealth of the wise man consists. But meanwhile let us consider the precious exchange. The children of Israel gave straw, which is burned with unquenchable fire, and received flour, in which that wise woman hid the leaven. They gave clay, which is wiped away, for it is written: Like the clay of the streets I will wipe them out (Ps. 17:43); and they received silver, which is the speech of the just man. For it is written: The tongue of the just man is silver tried by fire (Prov. 10:20). They gave bricks, which fall, for it is written: The bricks have fallen (Isa. 9:10); and they received gold, which is the good mind by which we serve the law of God. A good exchange, then; hence the Apostle says: Already you are filled, already you have become rich (1 Cor. 4:8). Let us acquire for ourselves these riches, with which to fill the spiritual treasuries of our soul; but the Lord himself gives us the grace to be able to snatch them from the Egyptians. Therefore the Apostle well says to the Hebrews: It is best to strengthen the heart with grace (Heb. 13:9). Rameses, then, is a good station.

2nd station, SUCCOTH. — The second departure of the children of Israel was to Succoth, and there, having left Egypt behind and pitching their tents, they had their second station. Therefore it says: And the children of Israel set out from Rameses and encamped in Succoth (Num. 33:5). The intention of the holy prophet Moses, who by God's command described the people's progress from Egypt to the Jordan, was not to note every single place at which it happened to them to turn aside on the whole journey, but only those in which some mysteries took place. Succoth is a city in the hill country, outside the land of Egypt, yet bordering on it, as we read in the book of Joshua son of Nun (Josh. 13:7). Succoth, in fact, is interpreted 'tents'. Hence, when Jacob parted from Esau, who had come to meet him as he returned from Mesopotamia, he returned, says Scripture, to the tents (Gen. 33:17), where another translation has: He returned to Succoth. And it adds there: And Jacob made houses for himself, and made tents for his livestock; for this reason he called the name of that place Tents. And there another translation says: He called the name of that place Succoth, that is, tents. In this station also they baked the flour, for it is said in the book of Exodus: And from the flour they made unleavened loaves baked under the ashes (Exod. 12:39); for it was not leavened, since the Egyptians had driven them out. In this station, moreover, the reckoning is made of the years during which Israel was in Egypt. For it says: But the dwelling of the children of Israel, in which they and their fathers dwelt in the land of Egypt, etc. (ibid., 40). In this station, finally, it is commanded that there should be among them a perpetual memorial of this deliverance from Egypt. For it says: Moses said to the people: Remember this day, on which you came out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage; for with a strong hand the Lord brought you out from here (Exod. 13:3). In this station, lastly, the solemnity of unleavened bread is prescribed, and the rite of eating unleavened bread. For it says: Six days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day [is] a feast to the Lord; nothing leavened shall appear there (ibid., 6). So much for the letter. As for the mysteries, we say that the departure of the children of Israel to Succoth, which is interpreted 'tents', signifies that whoever has had his station in Rameses, that is, in the commotion of penitence, must set out for Succoth, that is, to the tents, walking as it were by consideration. For just as one who is heading elsewhere and has no fixed house stays in tents — so what else is it to dwell in tents than to be a pilgrim? — as the Apostle testifies to the Hebrews, speaking of the fathers. For he says: Confessing that they were pilgrims and strangers on the earth (Heb. 11:13). And seeing himself a pilgrim on the earth, let him say with the Prophet: I am a stranger on the earth (Ps. 38:13). Let him likewise consider the Apostle's saying: We have here no lasting city (Heb. 13:14). Let him know, finally, that as long as he is in the body, he is a pilgrim away from the Lord; and so let him reject the things that are in the world, because they are the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. Let him follow the Apostle's counsel: Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle the things which all perish by their very use (Col. 2:21-22); but let him groan for the dwelling that is from heaven, always striving to please God. The baking of the unleavened loaves under the ashes teaches that, having purged out the old leaven of the wickedness of the philosophers and the malice of the Jews, he should feast on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Let each of us continually keep in memory that precept of the Lord, who says: Look and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees (Matt. 16:6), and let him not forget the warning of the Apostle: See that no one plunders you through philosophy and empty deceit (Col. 2:8). Next, at Succoth the reckoning of the years during which the people was in Egypt is ordered, because the penitent is told that he ought to cry like a swallow, and like a dove to meditate on his years in the bitterness of his soul (Isa. 38:14-15), and not to be without fear concerning the atonement of sin (Ecclus. 5:5), but to grieve and to say with the Prophet: And my sin is ever before me (Ps. 50:5). [It signifies] that he should not look back, craving his former vanities, like Lot's wife, and like the dog returning to its vomit. Rather, just as he prostituted himself to uncleanness and iniquity, so let him present his members to serve justice unto sanctification, so that as much as he glorified himself and lived in luxury, so much, correcting his errors and taking vengeance on himself, he may feel torment and grief. Finally a feast and perpetual solemnity of unleavened bread is prescribed, that is, perseverance in meditation and works is enjoined, because he who perseveres to the end will be saved. Hence the Apostle: Persevere in discipline, sons. The departure, then, from Rameses to Succoth is towards better things.

3rd station, ETHAM. — The third station is Etham. For withdrawing from Succoth, the children of Israel came to Etham, and pitching their tents there they completed their third halt. For it says: And setting out from Succoth, they encamped in Etham (Num. 33:6). Etham is a region between Egypt and the wilderness, in which is the town of Petra, in whose cave Samson lived when he was harassed by the Philistines: And he sat, it says, in the cave of the rock of Etham, which place was very strongly fortified, as Josephus testifies (Antiquities, ch. 10). This region was at the beginning of the wilderness; therefore it says: And it is part of the desert. The prophet David mentions this region, saying: You dried up the rivers of Etham (Ps. 73:15). In this station the Lord first appeared by night in a pillar of fire and by day in a pillar of cloud, showing the way to the people, as far as the land of their inheritance: And the pillar of cloud by day, it says, and the pillar of fire by night did not fail before all the people (Exod. 13:22). But since Etham means for us 'strength' — hence when Rehoboam was preparing to defend himself against Jeroboam, he built, it says, fortified cities, Etham and Tekoa (2 Chron. 11:6), that is, cities of strength — we are taught that when someone in the Succoth of this pilgrimage has resolved to persevere to the end in meditation and the exercise of good works, he ascends to Etham, that is, to strength; because the Lord himself gives power and strength to his people. Hence the Apostle said: I can do all things in him who strengthens me, Christ Jesus (Phil. 4:13). Indeed, through the cloud and the fire he opens the way for him and becomes the guide of his journey, until he sees the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. Let us too, then, ascend to Etham, so as to resist the devil, strong in faith.

4th station, OS EROTH. — The fourth station is called Os Eroth. Hence there follows: And setting out from Etham, they encamped at Os Eroth, which is opposite Baal-zephon and opposite Migdol (Num. 33:7). Os Eroth in another translation is called Pi-hahiroth; it is a village and suburb of Migdol, towards the Red Sea, as is found in the book of Exodus. In this station Pharaoh, indignant that Israel was leaving Egypt, assembled a great army and pursued them, saying: What have we done, that we let the children of Israel go, so that they should not serve us? (Exod. 14:5). And it adds: So Pharaoh yoked his chariots, etc. (ibid., 6). As to the moral sense: through Os Eroth, which is interpreted 'mouth of the nobles' (Jerome, Letter 127), it is shown that, having taken on strength in Etham, we ascend to Os Eroth, because we are ennobled in the Lord. And that Os Eroth is a village is not without mystery: that small things should be taken first, for the order is that one should come from small things to great. For immoderate prosperity at the beginning has always been dangerous, just as adversity has (Origen, Homily 27 on Numbers, in Rufinus' version). So just as we proceed through the suburb to the city, so we ascend through the lowest things to the highest. Then Baal-zephon, which is interpreted 'Lord of the North', signifies the devil, because he said, as the prophet Isaiah testifies: I will sit on a lofty mountain, above the high mountains towards the north (Isa. 14:13). Os Eroth, then, is opposite Baal-zephon, that is, opposite the devil, who always stands to oppose those going to the Jerusalem that is in heaven. Therefore the Apostle said: Put on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil (Eph. 6:11). The same is also signified by Pharaoh pursuing the people.

5th station, MARAH. — Marah is the fifth station. For thus it says: And setting out from opposite Os Eroth, they passed through the midst of the sea into the desert, and went a three days' journey through their desert, and encamped in Marah (Num. 33:8). Marah is a place in the desert of Shur, called by such a name on account of the bitterness of its waters; for thus it is written in the book of Exodus: And they came to Marah, and could not drink the water of Marah, for it was bitter; for this reason the name of that place was called Bitterness (Exod. 15:23). Concerning this station three things are to be considered: the departure, the station, and the working. The departure, because on this journey the children of Israel crossed the Red Sea dry-shod; for Scripture says: But the children of Israel went on dry ground in the midst of the sea, and the water was to them a wall on the right and a wall on the left (Exod. 14:22), while Pharaoh with his army was drowned in the mighty waters; for thus it is written of him: And the water returned and covered the chariots and the horsemen and all the army of Pharaoh, who had entered the sea after them, and not one of them was left (ibid., 28). The station, because they found bitter waters, and, perceiving their bitterness, could not drink, although they were tormented by great thirst. The working, because at the Lord's command Moses touched the waters with wood, and those which were before bitter, turned to sweetness, became drinkable, so that they could quench their thirst. By these things it is signified to us first that Pharaoh with his army, that is, the devil with a power so strong that, as it is written (Rev. [Job 41:24]), there is nothing on earth made like him, comes against those hastening to grace; but at last, as Pharaoh with his army is drowned in the mighty waters, so too the devil is cast into the lake of fire and sulphur. So let us not be so terrified by this as to desert. Next, in the station bitter waters are tasted, because while we are still in grace manifold bitternesses of tribulation remain. Hence John the apostle said: I John, your brother and sharer in tribulation (Rev. 1:9). Indeed, the apostle Paul said: If you are without discipline, you are bastards and not sons (Heb. 12:8). Finally, in the working, just as the Lord is present by his word, so that the waters grow sweet, so in tribulations he grants us his presence, as the Prophet says: I am with him in tribulation, that afflictions may grow mild (Ps. 90:15). Hence the prophet Isaiah proclaims: If you pass through water, I am with you, and the rivers shall not cover you; and if you pass through fire, you shall not be burned (Isa. 43:2). Therefore to Stephen the stones of the torrent were sweet, and to Lawrence the live coals were refreshment. Rightly, then, the Apostle says: We glory in tribulations (Rom. 5:3).

Sixth station, ELIM. – The sixth station is called Elim: for the children of Israel, withdrawing from Marah, came to Elim; there they halted, and there they set up their tents. Hence it says: And setting out from Marah, they came to Elim. Now in Elim there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees; and they encamped there by the waters (Num. 33:9). The same is read in the book of Exodus. But it is a fine order, and a happy progress of virtue, which always strives towards the best: out of darkness to light, out of hardships to happiness. See, the children of Israel, after the cruelties of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, after the perils of the sea and the desert, after the burning of a three days' thirst and the bitternesses of Marah, came at last to the palms, came to the springs. By this we are taught that those who are weighed down by harsh things are at last received by glad and pleasant places, since one does not come to rest except through toil, nor to joys except through sorrows. The people came to the palms, but first it endured very many hardships from the Egyptians. It came to the springs, but first it suffered three days' thirst and the bitterness of the waters. Yet even in these there is not yet the end of the journey, nor the final rest from toils, for heavier things still remain; but God, the steward of all things, who orders all things sweetly, inserts certain refreshments even in the journey itself, so that the soul, revived by them and with its strength restored, may return more readily to the remaining toils (Origen, Homily 27 on Numbers, in Rufinus' version). Then it must be observed that Elim is interpreted 'Rams'. And rams are the leaders of the sheep. Therefore the twelve springs and the seventy palms signify the leaders of the Christian flock: namely the twelve Apostles, of whom Luke writes thus: He chose twelve of them, whom he named Apostles (Luke 6:13); and the seventy Disciples, whom Saint Luke mentions elsewhere, saying: The Lord appointed seventy others also, and sent them two by two before his face (Luke 10:1). The Apostle sets down the distinction between them when treating of the Lord's appearances after his resurrection. For he says to the Corinthians: He was seen by Cephas, and after this by the eleven, and then he was seen by all the Apostles (1 Cor. 15[:5–7]). Yet all of these are leaders and teachers of the Lord's flock. Wherefore it is written of them: He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me (Luke 10:16). Let us, then, draw from such most abundant springs and drink; let us also pluck from the solid fruits of these palms of victory and eat eagerly, so that, refreshed by such food and drink, we may be found stronger for completing the remaining stations (Jerome, Letter 127).

Seventh station, THE RED SEA. – The seventh station is beside the Red Sea: for after the Red Sea had been crossed and the stations of Marah and Elim travelled through, a certain gulf of that same sea again met the children of Israel (Jerome, Letter 127). And because they put in there and set up tents, they are now said to encamp by the sea. For it says: And setting out from Elim, they encamped by the Red Sea (Num. 33:10). But observe that they see the sea, yet do not enter it; for it was enough to have entered and crossed it only once, since that sea was a figure of our baptism (Origen, Homily 27 on Numbers, in Rufinus' version), as the Apostle writes to the Corinthians, saying: That our fathers were all baptized in the cloud and in the sea (1 Cor. 10:2). But their baptism was in figure, ours in truth. And because baptism is not to be repeated, since it is written: One God, one faith, one baptism (Eph. 4:5), just as it was necessary to be baptized once, so too it was enough to have entered the sea once. Now, then, the sea again meets the people as it goes on to the promised inheritance, so that, seeing it and looking at its waves, it may go forward more cautiously, lest something worse befall it.

Eighth station, the desert of SIN. – The eighth station is the desert of Sin. Therefore it says: And setting out from the Red Sea, they encamped in the desert of Sin (Num. 33:11). But it must be observed that this whole wilderness, from the Red Sea as far as Mount Sinai, is called Sin (Jerome, Letter 127). In it the children of Israel had five mon- [...] in my members, fighting against the law of my mind (2 Cor. 11:2)? But it is one thing to endure wars bravely, another to be feebly overcome by wars. In the former virtue is exercised, so that no one should be puffed up; in the latter it is utterly extinguished, so that it does not survive. Next the law commanded the Levites to shave all the hair of their flesh (Num. 8:7), because those who are taken up into the divine service ought to appear clean before the eyes of God from all thoughts of the flesh, lest the mind bring forth unlawful thoughts, and these render the beautiful appearance of the soul unsightly, as if with hair growing out. After this two trumpets are also ordered to be made, by whose blast the peoples were to be moved to battle. For thus it is written of them to Moses: Make yourself two trumpets of beaten silver (Num. 10:2); and a little after: And when a broken blast has sounded, the camps shall move (ibid., 5). For the army is led by two trumpets, because through the two Testaments, or through the two precepts of charity, the people is called to the battle of faith. These are commanded to be made of silver for this reason, that the words of preachers may shine with the brightness of eloquence and not confuse the minds of the hearers by any obscurity of their own; and of beaten work for this reason, because it is necessary that those who preach the life to come should grow through the hammering of present tribulations. And it is well said: When a broken blast has sounded, the camps shall move; because, indeed, when the word of preaching is handled more finely and minutely, the minds of the hearers are roused more ardently against the struggles of temptations. From here the children of Israel now move on from Mount Sinai and pass over into the Graves of Craving.

Thirteenth station, THE GRAVES OF CRAVING. – The thirteenth station is held at the Graves of Craving. Therefore it says: And setting out from the desert of Sinai, they encamped at the Graves of Craving (Num. 33:16). This station took its name from an event. For the people, weary of the manna, craved meat, fish, melons, and the other incitements to gluttony that they had among the Egyptians, and stirred up a tumult against Moses. Wherefore the Lord, angered, sent a countless abundance of quails flying near the ground, with which they could fill their gluttony. But Scripture says: The meat was still in their teeth (Num. 11:33), that is, before it was digested, the Lord struck the people with a very great plague. And hence, it says, the name of that place was called the Graves of Craving, because there they buried the people that had craved (ibid., 34). From this we are taught that we who have left the way of life of the world, and have despised the Egyptian pots, that is, the heats of carnal desires, ought not to murmur against the heavenly bread, nor seek the poisonous things of the Egyptians, which are things of great meats, but seek the simple food of manna, that is, a pure and heavenly life. Otherwise, if after the precepts, the angelic food and the manna of the heavenly life or doctrine, we should wish once more to seek the Egyptian meats, which are the carnal pleasures of this world and the cravings of old vices, at once we shall be tormented, struck by the wrath of the Lord; our desires will be turned into tombs, so that we become whitewashed sepulchres, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, but inwardly are full of all filth. In this station Moses, by God's command, chose seventy elders from the people, to be his helpers in governing the people: And they shall bear with you, it says, the onset of the people, and you shall not bear them alone (Exod. 11:22). Upon these the Spirit afterwards descended, and they prophesied. This was done as a type, since the Holy Spirit poured himself into the Apostles on the day of Pentecost, so that they might be both wise for founding the Church and strong for ruling it: Take heed, it says, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to rule the Church of God (Acts 20:28). Thus the gift of heavenly power which once existed in Moses and in the Prophets appeared visibly upon the Apostles.

Fourteenth station, HAZEROTH. – The fourteenth station is completed at Hazeroth: for it adds: And setting out from the Graves of Craving, they encamped at Hazeroth (Num. 33:17). Of the same station it is also read elsewhere thus: From the Graves of Craving the people set out to Hazeroth (Num. 11:34[–35]). Here Aaron and his sister Miriam, because Moses had taken as wife a foreign Ethiopian woman, disparaged him quite insolently. Hence she, at once covered with the contagion of leprosy, was cast out from the company of the others until the time of her healing. This displayed a clear figure of a new mystery: namely that that priestly people of the fathers would rise up, out of jealousy over Christ our Saviour, against the Church gathered from the Gentiles. Through which, impure with the envy of faithlessness, it would come not to be admitted into the tabernacles of God, until the appointed time should become clear at which the fullness of the Gentiles would be completed, as the Apostle wrote to the Romans (Rom. 11:25). For only then will it be able to recover its former health, when the grace of the sevenfold Spirit has supported it towards pardon. But since Hazeroth is interpreted 'blessedness', one rightly comes from the Graves of Craving to this station, since unless a person has buried the cravings of the flesh, he will not be able to attain eternal blessedness. Therefore the Apostle says: Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 15:50).

Fifteenth station, RITHMAH. — The fifteenth station is called Rithmah. So it follows: And setting out from Hazeroth they encamped in Rithmah (Num. 33:18). But since elsewhere it is read: And after this the people set out from Hazeroth and encamped in the desert of Paran (Num. 13:1), lest the places of Scripture seem to contradict each other, it must be noted that from here as far as Ezion-geber all the stations, which are counted as eighteen — all, I say, following up to the thirty-second — are contained under the name of the desert of Paran. So this station is called Paran elsewhere, by the name of the wilderness common to it with many others; but Rithmah by its own name. Scripture commends Paran in another place, saying: God will come from the South, and the holy one from the shady mountain of Paran (Hab. 3:2). In this desert Moses, by God's command, sent twelve men to explore the land, who brought back a cluster of grapes, pomegranates and figs of the land (Num. 13:4). In this desert Dathan, Abiram and the sons of Korah with their households are swallowed by a chasm of the earth because of sedition. In this desert Aaron the priest, standing in the middle between the living and the dead, appeased the angry God by the offering of incense and checked the plague. In this desert Aaron's rod, placed dry in the tabernacle, by a miracle both sprouted and blossomed; and very many other things were done, as is read in the book of Numbers, though not distributed among the individual stations. By these we are taught mystically that the men sent to explore the fertile land, who made the people despair of the Lord's promised inheritance, displayed the image of the scribes and Pharisees. For as they were sent by Moses so that, examining the fruitfulness of the soil with careful consideration, they might encourage the people to obtain it, so these too were appointed through the Law and the Prophets, so that by searching the Scriptures they might watch for the Lord's coming, in which they could attain eternal life. But as those drew [the people] back from the hope of possessing the inheritance, or the people itself through their report estranged itself from God's promise, so these too by deceptions dissuaded the common people from believing in Christ the Lord. Therefore it is said against them: Woe to you who have taken away the key of knowledge: you yourselves have not entered, and those who were entering you have hindered (Luke 11:52). The cluster which they brought back is Christ. Therefore in the Song of Songs the Church says of Christ: My kinsman is to me a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engedi (Song 1:13). The pomegranate, because of its redness, is the blood of Christ. Hence Isaiah: Whence the redness of the garments from Bozrah? (Isa. 63:1). The fig, because of its sweetness, is the Gospel law: therefore, My yoke is sweet (Matt. 11:30). By Dathan and Abiram what else is signified than those who bring heresies and schisms into the Church? These, despising the authority of the priest and separating themselves from him and from the Church of God, dream up other churches, another altar, other customs, as Apollinaris, Novatian and the like; and, rejecting God's ordinance, they try to set up their own vanities. When at last the heretics and schismatics have been swallowed by the abyss of the earth, Aaron the priest — that is, Christ the Lord, a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek — is set in the middle to appease God: because he has an everlasting priesthood, always living to intercede for us (Heb. 7:24). The dry rod of Aaron, which afterwards sprouted by a miracle, is the flesh of Christ, which is called a rod by the prophet: A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse (Isa. 11:1). This, though dry, blossomed, because though dead it rose again.

Sixteenth station, RIMMON-PEREZ. — The sixteenth station is called Rimmon-perez. For it follows: And setting out from Rithmah they encamped in Rimmon-perez (Num. 33:19). This is the second station in the desert of Paran, which in our language is interpreted 'lofty division': because when someone has stayed in Rithmah, which is 'the mouth of one who sees', that is, has attained a perfect understanding of things, he comes to Rimmon-perez, that is, to the lofty division, by which he can separate heavenly things from earthly and lofty things from the lowest. And not undeservedly: for when the understanding has been invigorated and the knowledge of things grows, judgement is poured in, by which the eternal is distinguished from the temporal and the perpetual from the perishable. Therefore it is said through the Prophet: If you bring forth the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth (Jer. 15:19).

Seventeenth station, LIBNAH. — The seventeenth station is made in Libnah, which is why it adds: And setting out from Rimmon-perez they encamped in Libnah (Num. 33:20). By this station we are taught mystically that on the journey of this life we must be washed in body and clean in heart, as the Apostle writes to the Hebrews, saying: Let us draw near with a true heart in fullness of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with clean water (Heb. 10:22). For the interpretation of the word Libnah indicates this very thing: for Libnah means in Latin the same as 'whitening'. It is not, however, the whitening by which, blameworthily, both a whitewashed wall and whitewashed sepulchres are spoken of (Origen, Hom. 27 on Numbers, in Rufinus' version), but the one the Prophet prays for, saying: You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow (Ps. 50:9), which the Lord promises through the prophet, saying: If your sins are as scarlet, I will make them white as snow; and if they are like crimson, I will make them white as wool (Isa. 1:18). This whitening rises up powerfully from the brightness of judgement at Rimmon-perez and the clarity of visions at Rithmah, where the true Israelite completes his stations.

Eighteenth station, RISSAH. — The eighteenth station is completed in Rissah. Hence it adds: And setting out from Libnah they encamped in Rissah (Num. 33:21). By this station we are taught mystically that, although someone may seem to have advanced very much and to have achieved great progress, temptations nevertheless do not leave him. For the apostle Paul had already advanced so far that he was even caught up to the third heaven and heard secret, unspeakable things; nevertheless he felt himself still pressed by extraordinary temptations. Hence he complained: There was given me a goad of the flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me (2 Cor. 12:7). Yet the apostle James testifies that temptations of this kind are praiseworthy, saying: Count it all joy, brothers, when you fall into various temptations (Jas. 1:2); for these are applied to a person as a kind of safeguard. For just as meat, however choice it may be, goes bad unless it is sprinkled with salt, so too the soul, however perfect, grows slack unless it is salted with constant temptations (Origen, Hom. 27 on Numbers, in Rufinus' version). And this is so because Rissah is interpreted 'praiseworthy temptation'.

Nineteenth station, KEHELATHAH. — The nineteenth station is called Kehelathah, to which the children of Israel came on leaving Rissah. Hence it follows: And setting out from Rissah they encamped in Kehelathah (Num. 33:22). Kehelathah means in Latin 'rod', and signifies dominion, according to the verse: A rod of equity is the rod of your kingdom (Ps. 46:7). And rightly Kehelathah follows after Rissah: since when the soul has overcome temptations in Rissah, it comes out so strong that it ascends to Kehelathah, that is, gains dominion not only over its own lower powers but over the whole world. The Apostle had ascended here when he said: The world is crucified to me, and I to the world (Gal. 6:14). Let us too therefore encamp at this station, so that, crucifying the flesh with its vices and cravings and mortifying its deeds, we may say with the Apostle: The life I live in the flesh, I live in the faith of the Son of God (Gal. 2:20).

Twentieth station, SHAPHER. — The twentieth station is in Shapher. Therefore it says: And setting out from Kehelathah they encamped in Shapher (Num. 33:23). This station is a bold one; for it invites us to arduous things, namely to wars, and the harshest wars, against the strongest and fiercest enemies. Of these the Apostle said: Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers of this world, against the rulers of this darkness, etc. (Eph. 6:12). By these the same Apostle felt himself pressed and violence done to him; so he said: Unhappy man that I am, who will free me from the body of this death? (Rom. 7:24). And this is so because Shapher is 'the blast of a trumpet', or 'trumpeting', which is the signal for war. And not undeservedly; since the soul, seeing itself armed with so many and such great virtues in the preceding stations, cannot be restrained from coming forward into the open and not only offering itself for combat but showing itself ready; indeed, it also rouses the rest with the blast of trumpets, saying with the Prophet: Take up arms, bring shields into battle, saddle the horses, mount, horsemen, polish the lances (Jer. 46:4). Indeed it says with another prophet: Proclaim this among the nations, sanctify war, rouse the fighters, draw near, men of war (Joel 3:9). The fathers waged this war and won, as the Apostle relates to the Hebrews: They stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, became strong in war (Heb. 11:33). This station, therefore, is full of strength and spirit.

Twenty-first station, HARADAH. — The twenty-first station is Haradah; therefore it says: And setting out from Shapher they encamped in Haradah (Num. 33:24). This station too must be recalled with lengthy praises. For Haradah indicates 'made fit'. Here is a fine order; but the steps of those who advance must be observed, and the sequence of their progress examined. For when the soul has overcome temptations, it dares to press down its lower powers; and when it sees that it has command over these, it taunts the adverse powers, and not only does not fear their might but challenges them to combat. Now, secure of victory, it ascends to Haradah, that is, it glories in the Lord that it has been made fit, and says with the Apostle: Our sufficiency is from God, who has also made us fit ministers of the new Testament (2 Cor. 4:5, 6). Let us therefore pray God that we too may be able to reach Haradah and to keep our station there.

Twenty-second station, MAKHELOTH. — The twenty-second station is called Makheloth; therefore it adds: And setting out from Haradah they encamped in Makheloth (Num. 33:25). Makheloth is interpreted 'from the beginning', by which it is hinted that whoever strives toward perfection, or feels that he has in some way attained it, ought to look back to the beginning of things, on which all things depend, and to refer everything to it, and never to depart from it (Origen, in the place cited above). God is the beginning and the end, as is written in the Apocalypse: I am the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty (Rev. 1:8). Therefore all things must be led back to God. The prophet acknowledged him as the beginning when he said: Are you not from the beginning, O Lord my holy God? (Hab. 1:12). The Apostle acknowledged him, saying: I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named (Eph. 3:14).

Twenty-third station, TAHATH. — The twenty-third station is Tahath; therefore it follows: And setting out from Makheloth they encamped in Tahath (Num. 33:26). But since Tahath signifies in Latin 'long-suffering' or 'endurance', by it we are shown that whoever strives to advance in the way of God and to benefit others must suffer much and bear much with an even mind. For this reason it is said to the apostles: In your patience you will possess your souls (Luke 21:19). The Apostle invites us to endurance, setting before us the example of the fathers who went before, and of Christ. For he says: And therefore we also, having so great a cloud of witnesses laid upon us, putting aside every weight and the sin that surrounds us, let us run with patience to the contest set before us, looking to the author and finisher of faith, Jesus Christ (Heb. 12:1). For our Lord Jesus Christ showed us many examples of gentleness toward men and of enduring evils, as they are clearly recounted in the Gospels, so that we might follow in his footsteps, as the apostle Peter says (1 Pet. 2:21).

Twenty-fourth station, TERAH. — The twenty-fourth station is called Terah; for it follows: And setting out from Tahath they encamped in Terah (Num. 33:27). Terah is interpreted in Latin 'astonishment', in Greek ἔκστασις, which is a kind of intense wonder arising from the sight of difficult and unusual things. For when some unusual things, indeed things impossible to nature, present themselves to human sight, so that in investigating their cause the senses fail and reason gives way, the mind is astonished. Daniel expressed this most clearly, saying: I was astonished at the vision, and there was none who understood (Dan. 8:27). Hence when the people had seen that the paralytic who was carried by four men had at the Lord's word alone risen, taken up the bed on which he lay, and gone off to his house, they were astonished, because this was beyond human power. Therefore Saint Luke says: And astonishment seized them all (Luke 5:26). Treating of this, the prophet Jeremiah says: Astonishing and horrible things have been done in the land (Jer. 5:30). And because in these stations many splendid and wonderful works were performed, whose causes the human mind cannot grasp by reason, therefore at last one comes to Terah, that is, into astonishment; for so it is interpreted. Hence it is written: And all were astonished at the mighty works of God (Luke 9:44).

Twenty-fifth station, MITHCAH. — The twenty-fifth station is held in Mithcah; therefore it says: And setting out from Terah they encamped in Mithcah (Num. 33:28). Mithcah is called in Latin 'new death'. Now, so that it may be understood what the new death is, it must be observed that we read of a threefold death in the Scriptures. One is the death of the body, by which our earthly house of this dwelling, to use the Apostle's words, is dissolved, and the soul departs from the tent of the body. Of this the Apostle writes: It is appointed for men to die once (2 Cor. 5:1). By this Abraham and the prophets died, by this death we shall all die, and like water poured out on the ground we shall not be gathered up. Another is the death of the soul, by which the soul, consumed by the contagion of sin, dies, not indeed in its own substance, which cannot die, but in the life-giving grace of God. For through the guilt of sin, when God withdraws, the soul loses its spiritual life. Hence the Apostle says: She who lives [in pleasure] is dead (2 Tim. 5:6). And it is then said to die through sin, because the soul that sins, it shall die (Ezek. 18:4). It will die to the Lord, not through weakness of nature but through the guilt of fault, which is not a departure from this life but a fall into error. The third is the death of fault, by which the craving of the flesh dies so that the mind may live to God; of which the Apostle [says]: Our old man was crucified together [with him], so that the body of sin may be destroyed, that we may no longer serve sin (Rom. 6:6). And not undeservedly; for just as one dead to life is no longer liable to fault, so one reborn through grace ought no longer to serve sin. Of this death the Apostle speaks, saying: For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God (Col. 3:3). Rebuking such dead men, the same Apostle says: If you are dead with Christ from the elements of the world, why do you make decrees as though living in the world? (Col. 2:20). So one death is natural, another penal, the third spiritual. This last is designated by Mithcah, which is called 'new death', because it renews the old man and makes a new creature, as the Apostle says: The old things have passed away; behold, all things are made new (2 Cor. 5:17). So let us too make our station here, so that, dead to sins, we may live for ever to righteousness.

Twenty-sixth station, HASHMONAH. — The twenty-sixth station is named Hashmonah; for it says: And setting out from Mithcah they encamped in Hashmonah (Num. 33:29). Hashmonah is called in Latin 'hastening', which fits this station well. For when the soul, by the death of sin in the preceding station, has come out a new creature, it cannot stand still in spirit nor grow numb in idleness, but strives to go further and hasten its journey. Speed is most fitting for travellers: for this reason the people of the fathers are commanded to eat the passover, and in haste. Hence the apostles were commanded: Greet no one on the way (Luke 10:4). So in the book of Kings we read that Elisha enjoined Gehazi: Gird up your loins, he said, and take my staff in your hand, and go; and if you meet anyone, let him not bless him, and if anyone blesses you, do not answer him (4 Kgs. 4:29); for the work of God demands even very hurried haste. Cursed, says the prophet, is he who does the work of God negligently (Jer. 48:10). Therefore that disciple who ran ahead to the tomb faster than Peter (John 20:4) is praised beyond measure. In the way of God the progress must be swift indeed, so that the devil, who always stands at the right hand to oppose the saints, may be left no room to hinder the journey begun. Let us therefore, who through Mithcah are dead to sins and live to righteousness, not merely follow toward the prize of the heavenly calling, but run in Hashmonah, hastening to the contest set before us. For the shepherds came in haste and found the child Jesus (Luke 2:16).

Twenty-seventh station, MOSEROTH. — The twenty-seventh station is called Moseroth; for it says: And setting out from Hashmonah they encamped in Moseroth (Num. 33:30). Fittingly Moseroth now follows; for it signifies 'disciplines', so that whoever took up haste in Hashmonah may now wisely summon it to acquiring disciplines; and let every man be, as the apostle James teaches, swift to hear (Jas. 1:19). God is the author of this discipline: for it is said through the prophet: Who has gone up into heaven and taken her, and brought her down from the clouds? Who has crossed over the sea and found her, and will bring her for choice gold? There is none who knows her way, nor who considers her paths; but he who knows all things knows her, and has found her out by his prudence (Bar. 3:29 ff.). Therefore she must be sought from him, as the apostle James says: If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all abundantly (Jas. 1:5). She reveals God and his works. The discipline of God, says Solomon, is a teacher and a chooser of his works; her safeguard is the rod of correction. For it is written: Blows and corrections give wisdom (Prov. 29:15). We read in Numbers that a certain man was caught gathering wood on the sabbath day, was ordered to be set before Moses and the elders, and at last by God's command was punished with death, overwhelmed with stones: Let the man die the death, it says; all the congregation shall stone him with stones outside the camp (Num. 15:35). Some think this was done at this station. Hence the Apostle too said: Rebuke the sinner before all, so that the rest may have fear (1 Tim. 5:20). Let us therefore keep our station in Moseroth, that is, let us be held within the discipline of God by the mortification of corrections.

Twenty-eighth station, BENE-JAAKAN. — The twenty-eighth station is made in Bene-jaakan, for it says: And they departed from Moseroth and encamped in Bene-jaakan (Num. 33:31). Whoever keeps his station in the discipline of God must diligently spend all his zeal and all his effort so that not even the smallest part of God's law is violated and lost; and, as the Saviour says, so that not one iota, not one stroke passes from the Law (Matt. 5:18). For he must always keep in mind that saying of the Gospel: I tell you, you will not go out from there until you pay even the last farthing (Matt. 5:26). For just as a debt with interest is not cleared until the whole sum of the entire principal is paid, down to the smallest coin, by whatever kind of payment, so the penalty of sin is not dissolved except by the compensation of charity and the other virtues, or by strict satisfaction. Sin is not washed away, brothers, unless the guilty man is exercised by penalties long enough to pay the punishments of the error he committed. The apostle James said: Whoever keeps the whole Law but offends in one point has become guilty of all (Jas. 2:10). That sentence of God written in the Law must also be weighed: I am the Lord your God, a jealous God (Exod. 20:5). The law of God, then, must be examined with the most exacting scrutiny, and kept with the greatest diligence possible, lest we perhaps fall away from it. This the present station teaches us, for Bene-jaakan signifies 'straining'. And he who strains the law of God carefully watches that not even the least syllable or stroke slips through by negligence.

Twenty-ninth station, GIDGAD. — The twenty-ninth station is held on Mount Gidgad, for it says: And they departed from Bene-jaakan and encamped on Mount Gidgad (Num. 33:32). Temptation is for the soul a faithful guard, a strength, and an increase of virtue; for if the soul of the just man did not feel itself pressed by temptations from time to time, not only would it not remain on guard, but rather, as though overflowing with an abundance of graces, we would grow slack. This lesson is clearly had from holy Moses. When the people saw the torches and the smoking mountain and heard the voices, and fled from the Lord in terror, Moses said: Take heart, for God has come to you in order to test you, that his fear may be in you and you may not sin (Exod. 20:20). It is also called a strength; for the soul, recognising itself surrounded by manifold temptations, walks more warily and asks greater strength from the Lord, saying with the Prophet: Have mercy on me, O God, for many are warring against me (Ps. 55:2). And an increase of virtue, inasmuch as the soul, exercised by temptations, comes out purer. Therefore Solomon says in Proverbs: As silver and gold are tested in the furnace, so are chosen hearts with the Lord (Prov. 17:3). That the soul profits by temptations the holy apostle James also testifies, saying: Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life (Jas. 1:12). Temptations, then, are not to be fled but sought; whence the prophet David says: Test me, Lord, and try me (Ps. 25:2). So on those who advance in the way of the Lord temptations are thrust more frequently, that they may walk more warily and more fruitfully. This is what this station suggests to us, for Gidgad is interpreted 'temptation'. So, lest the traveller should overflow or slip because of the abundance of so many virtues of the earlier stations, this station follows the previous one.

Thirtieth station, JOTBATHAH. — The thirtieth station is held in Jotbathah; whence it follows: And they departed from Mount Gidgad and encamped in Jotbathah (Num. 33:33). By the trial of temptations the virtue of the just man, as was said at the previous station, shines out more conspicuous and brighter. Hence the apostle Peter too says: You will rejoice now, if you must be saddened by various temptations, so that the testing of your faith, much more precious than gold which is tested by fire, may be found (1 Pet. 1:6–7). Through it [virtue] also acquires greater grace; therefore it is written in the book of Wisdom: But virtue, once tested, rebukes the foolish (Wis. 1:3). Through it, too, virtue that lies hidden even in the midst of a crooked nation comes forth and shines; therefore the apostle Paul says to the Corinthians: There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest among you (1 Cor. 11:19). Goodness comes out of temptations more genuine, as silver comes purer out of the furnace of fire; for Scripture says: For silver is tested in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation (Sir. 2:5). Since, then, goodness comes out of temptation purer, as out of a furnace, Jotbathah, which is interpreted 'goodness', rightly follows now.

Thirty-first station, ABRONAH. — The thirty-first station is made in Abronah; therefore it says: And they departed from Jotbathah and encamped in Abronah (Num. 33:34). Although the just man may have come in this life even to perfect goodness, he does not halt in spirit or rest content with his present state; rather, passing through all things, he strains with burning desire toward better things. Hence the prophet David said: These things I remembered, and poured out my soul within me; for I shall pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God (Ps. 41:5). There indeed he will rest, there all his desire will be fulfilled. Therefore in another place the same prophet said: I shall be satisfied, Lord, when your glory appears to me (Ps. 16:15). In this life there is no rest, but a perpetual passing over. That is why in the Song of Songs the bridegroom, for the swiftness of his running, is likened to a roe and a young hart (Song 2:9); whence he also leaps upon the mountains and bounds over the hills. This station teaches us this, since Abronah is 'passing over': so that, although you have arrived at goodness through the previous station, all things must nevertheless be passed by; you must pass over to better things until you come to that good which is the highest, which satisfies every desire, and in which you are to remain for ever. (Origen, at the place cited.)

Thirty-second station, EZION-GEBER. — The thirty-second station is called Ezion-geber, where the children of Israel put in; whence it follows: And they departed from Abronah and encamped in Ezion-geber (Num. 33:35). This is the last station of the children of Israel in the desert of Paran; for, as we said above, that wilderness, encompassing very many stations, extends as far as here. It is interpreted 'counsels of a man'. And this fits the intention well: for he who has completed so many stations, has entered into the recesses of so many virtues, has felt the breathings of so many spiritual gifts, has exercised himself in so many pursuits of perfection, has now ceased to be a child in understanding, has now reached the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, has now grown into a perfect man. And therefore he has attained the counsels of a man, so that he may say with the Apostle: But when I became a man, I put away the things of a child (1 Cor. 13:11). Rather, he has attained deep counsel, for Solomon says in Proverbs: Counsel in the heart of a man is deep water (Prov. 20:5). Of this counsel the wise man said: Do nothing without counsel, and in doing it you will not regret it (Sir. 32:24). It is not that counsel of which the Lord complains through the prophet, saying: Woe, apostate sons! Thus says the Lord: You have taken counsel, but not through me, and made a pact, but not through my Spirit (Isa. 30:1). But that of which the wise man [says]: The knowledge of the wise will abound like a flood, and his counsel like a pure fountain of life (Sir. 21:16), which guards from evil; for good counsel will guard you, and holy thought will preserve you. Let us therefore go here without hesitation, and eagerly pitch our tents here, so that we may be able to praise God with our whole heart, as David [did], in the council of the just and in the congregation (Ps. 110:1).

Thirty-third station, SIN. — The thirty-third station is in the desert of Sin; therefore it adds: And they departed from Ezion-geber and encamped in the desert of Sin (Num. 33:36). The eighth station above is also called by the same name; for it says: And they departed from the Red Sea and encamped in the desert of Sin. But it should be noted that this place is different from that one; therefore it is added below: From the desert of Sin, this is Kadesh (Num. 20:1). And elsewhere, while the people were staying at this station, Moses, sending messengers to the king of Edom, said: And now we are in the city of Kadesh, on the edge of your borders (ibid., 14). The prophet David mentions it, saying: And the Lord will shake the desert of Kadesh (Ps. 28:8). Here Miriam, the sister of Moses, met her day: she died and was buried, as is read above. Josephus too describes this, saying: At that time, then, the end of life took his sister Miriam, when she had completed the fortieth year since she left Egypt; and they buried her publicly with great splendour (Antiquities, book 4, ch. 4). Here, finally, the people suffered from a lack of water; and so in anger they rioted against Moses. By him a rock was struck, at God's command, with the wonderful rod, and water flowed abundantly; whence the craving of thirst was taken away from all who drank.

The 34th station, HOR. The thirty-fourth station is on Mount Hor; for it says: And they departed from the desert of Sin, this is Kadesh, and encamped on Mount Hor near the land of Edom (Num. 33:37). While the children of Israel were staying at Kadesh in the desert of Sin, Moses sent envoys to the king of the Idumaeans, so that he might grant him and his people a way through his territory; they were to assure him that [Moses] would not ask even for water to be supplied to him without payment. But he, not consenting to the request or granting passage, replied: You shall not pass through me; otherwise I will come out against you in war (Num. 20:18). Therefore the people, by God's command, as is found in Deuteronomy, turned aside from him; and leaving Kadesh they came to Mount Hor, and had this station of which we read (ibid., 27 ff.). There, according to the Lord's command, Aaron went up Mount Hor with his brother Moses and his son Eleazar; and there Moses, at God's word, stripped Aaron of his priestly vestments and at once clothed with them his son Eleazar, to whom the high priesthood fell by reason of age, while the whole people, standing opposite, looked on in wonder. And there, when Aaron had ended his life and was gathered to his people, his son Eleazar was declared priest in place of his father Aaron. This station, then, is memorable.

The 35th station, ZALMONAH. The thirty-fifth station is held at Zalmonah; for there follows: And they departed from Mount Hor and encamped at Zalmonah (Num. 33:41). The people, leaving Mount Hor, did not follow the straight road they had begun, but, going around the land of Edom, took the way towards the Red Sea, so that, according to the word of the Lord, they would not attack their brothers in war nor harm them at all; for he says: Do not move war against them (Deut. 2:5). Wearied, then, by so many windings of the road, and sick of the manna, [the people] spoke, it says, against God and Moses. Therefore the Lord in anger sent among the people venomous and deadly serpents, which killed with their bite; whence a very great many people perished. The Apostle too mentions them, saying: Nor let us tempt Christ, as some of them tempted, and perished by serpents (1 Cor. 10:9). Then, when Moses prayed for the destruction of the serpents, God answered: Make yourself a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign; and everyone who is bitten and looks at it shall live (Num. 21:8). Moses did according to the Lord's command, and the people were freed from the plague. Now since Zalmonah is interpreted 'shadow', this event fits the station well. For the serpent hung on wood was a type and shadow of Christ hanging on the cross for our salvation, as he himself explains in the Gospel, saying: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish, but have eternal life (John 3:14). Let us, then, frequent this station, so that we may look upon Christ hanging on the cross for the salvation of the world; for it is a saving [station].

The 36th station, PUNON. The thirty-sixth station is called Punon; for it says: And they departed from Zalmonah and encamped at Punon (Num. 33:42). The holy apostle James, in an extended discourse, counts control of the tongue among the things that are no less necessary to a man than difficult, saying: If anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man, able to lead about with a bridle even the whole body (Jas. 3:2). See, we put bridles in the mouths of horses to make them obey us, and we turn about their whole body. See also ships: though they are so great and are driven by strong winds, they are turned about by a small rudder wherever the impulse of the steersman wills. So too the tongue is a small member, and boasts great things. See how great a forest a small fire sets ablaze. And the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity (Eccl. 28:28–29); and the rest that the holy apostle sets out for you to the purpose. If so many evils threaten a man from the tongue, who will dare to say that it does not need control? Therefore the Wise Man commands this, when he says: Hedge your property about with thorns, and make doors and bolts for your mouth; melt down your silver and your gold, and make a balance for your speech, and make a gate and a bolt for your mouth (ibid., 12). But since a balance, gate and bolt for the tongue did not readily come to hand, the same Wise Man said: Who will set a guard over my mouth, and a seal upon my lips? (Eccl. 22:33). But the prophet David, recognising that these gifts are granted by the Lord, prayed to the Lord in these words: Set, Lord, a guard on my mouth, and a door of enclosure around my lips (Ps. 140:3). Control of the tongue has its seat in this station. For Punon is interpreted 'sparing of the mouth'. Let us too, then, take care to have our station here, so that we may know what, when, how and to whom it is fitting to speak; and that our mouth may meditate wisdom, and our tongue speak judgement (Ps. 36:30).

The 37th station, OBOTH. The thirty-seventh station is called Oboth, where the children of Israel next arrived; for there follows: And they departed from Punon and encamped at Oboth (Num. 33:43). Of this station we read elsewhere: And the children of Israel departed and encamped at Oboth (Num. 21:11). But it should be noted that by common consent the greater and more destructive temptations by which the soul is assailed in this life are thought to be the illusions of demons and the deceptions of magicians and soothsayers. For these, by sorcery and magic arts, in order to banish the worship of the Godhead from the hearts of men, claim to do things that are possible only to the divine nature. Hence they dare to resist its power continually. But in the end, when their vanities are exposed and their arts overthrown, the divine power always prevails. The magicians dared to resist Moses before Pharaoh, and strove to make their rods into serpents. But in the end the rod of Moses, by the providence and power of God, was turned into a snake, and leaping upon the magicians' serpents, devoured them at once (Exod. 7:10 ff.). For these things were done by Moses not by error, not by deception, but in truth; therefore they stood firm by a wonderful power. We read also in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 13:8 ff.) that while the apostle Paul was preaching before the proconsul Sergius, who wished to hear the word of God, Elymas the magician, it says, resisted, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. At length, when he was rebuked by the Apostle, he was made blind, so that, it says, going about he sought someone to lead him by the hand. Therefore in the law it is especially commanded to beware of dealings with them; for it says: The soul that follows ventriloquists or enchanters, to go whoring after them, I will set my face against that soul, and destroy it from among its people (Lev. 20:6). This station is kept for the destruction of magicians: for Oboth is interpreted 'against magicians'. Let us too, then, go to Oboth and set up our tents there, so that, dwelling in the protection of the God of heaven, we may not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies by day, nor the thing that walks about in darkness, nor the attack and the noonday demon (Ps. 90:2, 6).

The 38th station, IYE-ABARIM. The thirty-eighth station is called Iye-abarim; for so it is found: And they departed from Oboth and encamped at Iye-abarim, in what is beyond, on the borders of Moab (Num. 33:44). Of this station we read more clearly in another place: And departing, it says, from Oboth, they encamped at Iye-abarim, in the desert that faces Moab, towards the sunrise (Num. 21:11). On this account it should be remembered that the Idumaeans, as we said above, refused in hostile fashion to grant the children of Israel passage through their lands. Hence, turning away from them, they were forced to go around the borders of the Moabites. Thus it is said that they came to the borders of Moab towards the east. Iye-abarim, moreover, means 'heap of passing stones', which is the Church of the just. For the passing stones are the just. They are called stones because of their firmness; of them the apostle Peter writes, saying: And you yourselves, like living stones, are built up into a spiritual house (1 Pet. 2:5).
