Firmness is rightly ascribed to the just, because they neither waver nor are carried about by every wind of doctrine; hence in the Gospel they are compared to a house founded upon firm rock, upon which the rain came down, the floods came, the winds blew, and it did not fall (Matt. 7:25). They are also called passing, because, according to the Apostle, they confess that they are guests and strangers upon the earth (Heb. 11:13). Finally, the Church is rightly called a heap of stones, because she is the pillar and foundation of truth (1 Tim. 3:15). Let us too, then, have our station at Iye-abarim, so that, according to the apostle Paul, we may hold fast the hope set before us, as an anchor of the soul, safe and firm, and entering into the inner part behind the veil (Heb. 6:19); and so that, according to the apostle Peter as well, knowing beforehand, we may beware lest, led away by the error of the wicked, we fall from our own firmness (2 Pet. 3:17).

39th station, DIBON-GAD. — The thirty-ninth station is held at Dibon-gad; for so we read: And they set out from Iye-abarim and encamped at Dibon-gad (Num. 33:45). But concerning this station something very different seems to be read in another place; for it is written: And departing from Oboth, they encamped at Iye-abarim, in the desert that is opposite Moab, towards the rising of the sun. From there they departed and encamped in the valley of Zared; so it says there (Num. 21:11). If, then (Origen, at the place cited), they encamped in the valley of Zared, you will say: How [then] at Dibon-gad? But there the general place is expressed, here the particular one. For Dibon-gad is near the valley of Zared, which lies between the borders of the Amorites and the Moabites. Mystically, Dibon-gad signifies 'a beehive of temptations'. By this we are taught that although the just man may be close to perfection, even to the highest, temptations are nevertheless not lacking to him. This is a precaution of divine providence, so that we may not seize from good successes an occasion for turning aside from what is right. Hence Job said: Blessed is the man whom the Lord has rebuked: do not refuse the reproof of the Almighty (Job 5:17). And even if, while we are in the flesh, temptations seem bitter to us, they nevertheless profit us wonderfully for the life to come, as the Apostle says: All discipline, indeed, for the present seems to be not a matter of joy but of sorrow; but afterwards it will yield the most peaceful fruit of justice to those who have been trained by it (Heb. 12:11). Let us then draw near, and hasten to enter this station, knowing that we are at times rebuked by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with this world (1 Cor. 11:32). Let us also have sure hope that God will not let us be tempted beyond what we are able, but will make with the temptation a way out, so that we may be able to bear it (1 Cor. 10:13).

40th station, ALMON-DIBLATHAIM. — The fortieth station is made by the children of Israel at Almon-diblathaim; for so it is written: And they set out from Dibon-gad and encamped at Almon-diblathaim (Num. 33:46). This name Almon-diblathaim, as it is double, so also indicates two things, namely 'contempt of figs', that is, contempt of earthly sweetness; for figs show sweetness. Hence the prophet Jeremiah saw good figs, very good (Jer. 24:3). And our Saviour, being hungry, leaving behind the bitterness of the scribes and Pharisees, went up to a fig tree, so as to find at least some sweetness among the common people; and when he found nothing but leaves only, he cursed it, saying: May fruit never grow from you (Matt. 21:19). Contempt of earthly delights, then, is above all necessary for one hastening to heaven. For unless we disregard the allurements of pleasures and the things that seem to delight on earth, we cannot raise ourselves up to heavenly things. Therefore the Apostle admonishes, saying: Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things upon the earth (Col. 3:2). Indeed, to set the mind on earthly things is shame. As the Apostle writes: Their glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things (Phil. 3:19). But since our citizenship is in heaven, we who have risen with Christ (ibid., 20), let us with all eagerness of heart trample the allurements of the world and enter the tents of this station, seeking the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God (Col. 3:1); and let us strive, whether absent or present, to please the Lord our God.

41st station, ABARIM. — The forty-first station is made by the children of Israel in the mountains of Abarim; for it follows: And they set out from Almon-diblathaim and encamped on the mountains of Abarim, opposite Nebo (Num. 33:47). But what is read about this station in another place seems very far from this. For it says: They encamped in the valley of Zared; going down from there, they encamped beyond the Arnon in the desert, which stands out from the borders of the Amorites (Num. 21:12-13). From these words it seems that the children of Israel had their station after Almon not in the mountains of Abarim but in the desert beyond the Arnon. But there is no discrepancy, since Abarim is in the desert beyond the Arnon. What Scripture expressed elsewhere under a general name, then, it has expressed here under the particular name. (Hence it adds: For the Arnon is at the borders of Moab, among the Amorites; and there we have Mount Abarim, at whose foot, near the Amorites, the river Arnon flows. Mount Abarim is said to be 'beyond the Arnon' not with respect to the crossing of the Hebrews, but with respect to the position of the holy land, as is Moses' custom in this description; for in the book of Deuteronomy we read: These are the words which Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan, in the desert, towards the west (Deut. 1:1). Yet Moses never crossed the Jordan at all; he was therefore on this side with respect to the route of the Hebrews, but beyond with respect to the position of the holy land. At this station Moses sent envoys to Sihon, king of the Amorites, asking him to grant passage to him and the people through his lands, entirely without any harm to his people: We will pass, they say, through your land; we will not turn aside either into field or into vineyard, nor will we drink water from a well; we will go by the king's road (Num. 21:22). But Sihon, refusing this altogether, answered harshly; indeed, with a strong army in arms, he at once went down to the river Arnon, where Israel was about to cross, to block the way and resist them as they attacked. But it came about by divine power that, the king being killed in battle, the Hebrews struck down the people of the Amorites with the slaughter of the sword, and laying waste their lands, plundered them. Meanwhile Og, king of Bashan, to bring help to his friend the Amorite, armed huge forces, with which he advanced to attack Israel as an enemy. But Israel, fighting with help from above, both killed the king himself in battle and destroyed his whole army, and finally subdued all their land; whence, with a notable victory, it carried off great abundance of riches. All of this Josephus has written out at length (Antiquities, book 4, ch. 4).

42nd station, at the JORDAN. — The forty-second station is held in the plains of Moab by the Jordan; therefore it says: And they set out from the borders of Abarim and came to the west of Moab, above the Jordan near Jericho; and there they encamped by the Jordan, from Beth-jeshimoth as far as Abel-shittim, in the west of Moab (Num. 33:48-49). In another place Scripture mentions the same station, saying: And the children of Israel departed and encamped to the west of Moab, by the Jordan, near Jericho (Num. 22:1). This, finally, is the last station of this long and laborious journey of the children of Israel described by Moses through the word of God. Although many things worthy of record were said and done at it, we shall nevertheless relate only these few. First, Balak, king of the Moabites, seeing the children of Israel advancing with such growth, and their affairs prospering with such favourable successes, conceived great fear for his own affairs, as appears in what he said beforehand to the people of Midian. For he says: Now this multitude will lick up all who are round about us, as a calf licks up the living things of the field (ibid., 4). Therefore, not daring to attack them openly in arms, he resolved, so that at least they might not become more powerful, to resort to secret arts. So he summoned the magician Balaam to him and asked him to curse and destroy the people with imprecations and his evil arts. This he was never able to obtain from him, either by persuasion or by gifts, since divine providence stood in the way; on the contrary, the Lord opening his mouth, he rather prayed good things for the people and foretold happy successes: How beautiful, he says, are your houses, Jacob, your tents, Israel, like shady valleys, like gardens beside a river, and like tents which the Lord has pitched (Num. 24:5-6); and further on: Those who bless you shall be blessed, and those who curse you shall be cursed; again: A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall arise out of Israel (ibid., 17). Next, because the people, through love of the Midianite women, had abandoned the true God and turned aside to idols, Phinehas son of Eleazar and grandson of Aaron, zealous with zeal for the Lord of hosts, before iniquity could rage more strongly through licence, killed with a drawn dagger, in public, a Hebrew and a Midianite woman caught in fornication and brought before Moses; provoked by his example, many seized arms and rose up against the fornicators, and twenty-four thousand men were slain in slaughter that day. Therefore, the fornicators being destroyed, God was reconciled with the people: And the plague, it says, ceased from the children of Israel (Num. 25:8). Moreover, because the land of the Canaanites, which the children of Israel were making for, to possess it by the word of God, now loomed close at hand, and they were already almost grasping the borders of the holy land, which had fled from them for forty years and more; and because it was granted them to take it only with armed hand and unbroken strength: for that reason Eleazar the priest, by God's command, resolved to make a new count of the people fit for war, in which, besides the tribe of Levi, appointed for the special worship of God, and the women, six hundred and one thousand seven hundred and thirty men, from twenty years and upwards, ready for wars, as Scripture says, were numbered. Very many other things concerning religion and the worship of God, and also the governing of the commonwealth in war and peace, Moses and Eleazar the priest set in order at this station (Num. 26:51); these we judge should now be passed over, so that they may not draw out our reading too long, or because we have treated them often in other places. Yet we have not thought it right to pass over in silence that Moses, recognising through the word of God that his last day was at length upon him, having declared, by God's command, Joshua son of Nun as his successor and the leader of the people, and having set out the blessings and curses (Deut. 27ff.) which the keepers or transgressors of the divine law would incur, and also having foretold to each tribe what would befall them individually, went up onto Mount Nebo; and from there he surveyed with his eyes, and considered with his mind, the broad and excellent country of the Canaanites, a land indeed flowing with milk and honey, promised to the fathers in repeated oracles, lying opposite Mount Nebo; and, to use the Apostle's words (Heb. 11:13), he greeted it from afar. When this was done, the Lord said to him: I have shown this land to your eyes, but you shall not enter it (Deut. 34:4). And at once, by the word of God, he died, and was buried in the valley; and no one knows his grave to this day. This is the end of Moses, and of the stations of the people set out in order by God's command. For the rest, some mystical points would now need explaining, had we not scattered most of them through the present treatise and explained others in other places. Finally, we have judged it worth the effort to observe that this whole passage is recorded for everyone, and this whole course is set before us to be completed, so that, coming at last to the Jordan, the river of God, we may be watered by the waves of divine wisdom; so that, purified in all things, we may by God's mercy at last be able to enter the land of promise and to say with the Apostle: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; and so that the crown of justice, which the Lord, the just judge, will render on that day to those who love his coming (2 Tim. 4:7-8), may be laid up for us through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom with the Father and the Holy Spirit be all honour, glory and eternity for ever and ever. Amen.
ADVICE TO THE READER ON THE FOLLOWING COMMENTARIES.

As much as there was agreement once, over many centuries, that the following Work should be attributed to Saint Ambrose, so with equal agreement all who are now counted learned men want it taken away from him. For from as early as the ninth century Hincmar (Treatise on the Divorce of Lothair, etc.), the Church of Lyons (Bibliotheca Patrum vol. 4, part 2), the third Council of Aachen (year 862, ch. 8), Amalarius, Prudentius, Haymo and many other authors of the same time quoted much from these very Commentaries under Ambrose's name. Rabanus, Hincmar's contemporary, in his Exposition of the Pauline epistles collected from the Fathers, adduces very many passages on the first five epistles as truly Ambrose's, which in fact are found in these Commentaries of ours. From there too Sedulius transferred some things into his explanation of the earlier epistles of the same Paul, ascribing Ambrose's name once. Lanfranc also, in his Compilation, attributes to the holy Doctor the fragments that he borrowed from this Work. Finally, this Work was accepted as Ambrose's by Gratian, Peter Lombard, Ivo of Chartres and countless others. Yet since so universal an opinion seemed not altogether certain to Erasmus, Turrianus and others, thereafter, the matter having been examined more deeply, all with one vote rejected it.

Therefore we would seem to be doing what has already been done if we lingered longer in proving a matter so thoroughly established. We will not, however, pass over in silence that the style of the Work differs so greatly from Ambrose's that it is plainly a wonder that this difference was detected so late. Nor is the disagreement between the teaching of the two authors any slighter; for in Ambrosiaster there occur not only certain extraordinary opinions, enormously at odds with the views of the true Ambrose, but also in asserting the most catholic doctrines the two do not sufficiently agree; and in refuting what the Arians used to object, he employs answers which the holy Doctor neglects, proposing quite different ones. Besides this, it would be useless to point out what is obvious to everyone, namely that this writer was wholly a stranger to the Greek language. And what if we add that it is not so very clear whether Ambrose wrote Commentaries on Paul at all? But even granting that the holy man did publish such an exposition, it is at least quite credible that it had already perished in Cassiodorus' time; for this can be inferred from his following words: It is also said, he says, that blessed Ambrose left an annotated codex of all the epistles of Saint Paul, filled with a most delightful exposition; which, however, I have not yet been able to find, etc. (On the Institution of Divine Letters, ch. 8).

The whole difficulty, then, lies in tracking down the true parent of this Work. Some have held that it was a compiler who stitched together a patchwork from shreds torn from Chrysostom and Jerome. Others hold that the prologues prefixed to the several expositions belong to an inept patcher, who pilfered many scraps chiefly from Jerome. Yet on comparing the Works of those same Fathers we have by no means found this. On the contrary, we have quite often noticed that this author dissents from their opinions, offers other explanations, sometimes cites the Apostle's text not in the way they usually do; and finally, wherever he agrees with them, this has happened because it is impossible for those who labour at commentaries on the same book to disagree everywhere. Nor, however, shall we deny that our author seems to have borrowed certain things from Jerome; but we do not think he is therefore to be held a compiler, in the sense in which they understand it. Of the others who have tried to discover the author of these Commentaries, those who attributed them to Remigius laboured in vain. For both in the Bibliotheca Patrum and in not a few manuscripts there survive works of Remigius plainly different from ours. There have also been those who contended that this commentary belonged either to Julian or to some other Pelagian. But likewise writers have been found who thought its author should be freed from that mark, and that if anything perhaps occurs there which could favour those heretics, it should be put down to the fact that, since he wrote before their heresy arose, he spoke less cautiously and considerately. The last, finally, and more common opinion is that of those who say the true Author of this Work is Hilary, deacon of the Roman Church, who, having adhered to the Luciferian schism, was handled in so harsh a style by Jerome (Dialogue against the Luciferians, after the middle). But since there are also those who contradict this view, it must be weighed more carefully.

We shall observe first that there is scarcely any Work of the true Ambrose of which more copies of every age from the last eight hundred years are found than of this Ambrosiaster; but that some of them differ from others not a little. Indeed, in the library of Corbie there is one contained in two volumes, than which we have been allowed to see none finer, whether you consider antiquity or elegance of script. But although it contains, under Ambrose's name, Commentaries on all the epistles of Paul except the one inscribed to the Hebrews, it agrees with other manuscripts and printed copies only on the first three epistles, and differs on the rest. Rabanus Maurus, going further in his Commentary collected from the Fathers, credits to Ambrose's name all the things he quotes taken from Ambrosiaster on the first five epistles; but whatever he inserts under the holy Doctor's title on the remaining ones can be found only in the Corbie codex. Ivo of Chartres also cites (Decretum part 16, ch. 84) some words from the prologue of the exposition of the epistle to Philemon, which you would find only in Rabanus and in the Corbie codex.

Whoever considers all this attentively will cease to wonder that many things are missing in our Author which Lanfranc quotes as from Ambrose's Commentaries on the Apostle; and he will easily notice that the name of Ambrose was given by copyists to various expositions of the Pauline epistles. It must be added besides that the same scribes took great licence at least on the first three epistles; since it is probable that long fragments were not seldom inserted there by them which are not found in the older manuscripts, as will be noted in the variant readings. And from this a strong conjecture can be drawn against the integrity and genuineness of this Work; and it is recognised to be no matter of ready judgement to affirm whether it is the labour of one author or of several.

For the rest, if we deny that it is the work of several, it will at the same time seem necessary to admit that it is the work of an ancient commentator. For what he says (On 1 Timothy, ch. 3) of the Church whose ruler today is Damasus must either be attributed to an interpolator (and it certainly does not savour of the usage of those times, nor is it necessary to the sense), or it will become plain that the same author wrote his Commentaries before the year 384, in which that same pope ceased to live. This can also be confirmed by his testifying there that the Marcionites still survived, although, he says (ibid., ch. 4), they have almost died out. It is certain indeed from Epiphanius (Heresy 42) and Theodoret (Compendium of Heretical Fables, book 1, ch. 24) that these heretics were extinguished quite late; but it is also established that in many places they readily passed over to the party of the Manichaeans, who are mentioned more frequently here. In passing it also seems worth observing that in this Work mention is made (On 2 Timothy, ch. 3) of a certain law promulgated by Domitian against them, which you would find only in the Collection of Mosaic and Roman Laws. What marks the Author's antiquity still more is that he does not pass over the Patricians (On 1 Timothy, ch. 4), whom Philaster (Book of Heresies) and Augustine mention as surviving, since they by no means lasted beyond the fifth century. Moreover, of the other heretics, whom he attacks in very great number, none somewhat more recent is mentioned. And since he applies himself more often and more laboriously to refuting the Donatists, Novatians, Arians and Photinians than others, this is no doubt an indication that the later heretics, say the Nestorians and the rest of the following times, had not yet emerged, but that the heresies of those we have just named were then flourishing. Add to this that this writer now and then cites the Apostle's text from a version other than the one we now use, and that the testimonies of the Old Testament are taken from the version of the Seventy Elders. To the same point tends the fact that of ecclesiastical authors he uses passages only of Tertullian, Cyprian and Victorinus, the last of whom matched Damasus in antiquity. Lastly, the same age can similarly be established from the fact that, in the baptism of the sick and on not a few other heads, he finely represents the church discipline of those times.

All that we have recounted here seems to support the view of those who hold that these Commentaries were published by Hilary; they were led to this opinion by the testimony of Augustine, writing thus against the Pelagians (Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, book 4, ch. 4): For holy Hilary too understood thus what is written: In whom all have sinned; for he says: In whom, that is, in Adam, and the rest, which can be read word for word in this Work. And these words, they say, can fit no one but Hilary the Deacon, who himself indicates that he was a contemporary of Damasus. It has indeed been objected that rebaptisers are sharply attacked by this Author, whereas Hilary was tainted with that same charge; and moreover that Augustine would never have given the title 'saint' to this Hilary, who he well knew had withdrawn from the Church in schism. But it is answered that he did not think all heretics should be rebaptised, but only the Arians, and that by this distinction he shows he was led to that opinion for no other reason than that these heretics, not believing rightly about the Trinity, also used an illegitimate form in baptism; and so nothing prevented him from attacking heretics who rebaptised catholics. They think they satisfy the second objection if they deny that the honorific title mentioned is proof that Saint Augustine is to be understood of Hilary the Luciferian; rather, they say, it is to be inferred from it either that this deacon never made a secession from the universal Church, keeping, that is, peace and communion with its head, blessed Damasus; or that he at last, before departing from the living, returned to favour with the catholics. But Jerome is plainly contrary to this sort of answer, since he speaks of Hilary as separated, not from some bishops or only for a time, but from all catholic fellowship through the whole course of his life (Dialogue against the Luciferians, after the middle). Against this opinion there is also the fact that Hilary, being a deacon of the Roman Church, would not have spoken of it as though a stranger or outsider. For how could he have written of his own Church: Now there should be seven deacons, and some presbyters, so that there may be two to each church (On 1 Timothy, ch. 3)? For since, in the reign of Diocletian (Optatus, book 2), there were already forty basilicas in the City, it was necessary that not some presbyters but at the very least eighty be ordained there.

Nor is there any doubt that these very reasons put it into Petavius's mind to assign the same Commentaries to a Hilary indeed, but to one other than the Luciferian, whoever he may at last have been. And certainly (Ughelli, Italia sacra, vol. 1, part 2, p. 6), even if we did not have Hilary, bishop of Pavia under Damasus, famed for holiness and for zeal against the Arians, to whom they could perhaps be ascribed, there still survive many writings whose authors are known only by name, and whom we would be wholly ignorant of, had it not happened by chance that they were once named by someone else. But although these points cannot be denied in general, it can nevertheless be objected that Augustine, when fiercely attacking the Pelagians who impugned the doctrine of original guilt, would not have used the testimony of that author who, though in places he seems to acknowledge it, yet at times puts forward the contrary; who is judged by very weighty and highly approved theologians to favour the Pelagians openly; and who in at least one place is plainly declared a Semipelagian by Giustiniani of the Society of Jesus, a most learned man (Commentary on 1 Corinthians, ch. 14). What if we add to this the other errors too which are found here and there in the same Commentaries? Certainly their author cannot be defended from having held with Origen (from Estius's Commentary on Ephesians, ch. 3) that it lies in the will of the demons to spring back from error. It is also well established that he maintains (On 1 Corinthians, ch. 7) that a husband is fully permitted, having put away his wife for adultery, to marry another, but denies that a wife separated from an adulterous husband may enter into marriage with another. Nor are these things sound enough either: that he denies that woman was made in the image of God (On 1 Corinthians, chs. 11 and 14, and on Colossians, ch. 3), that bishops hold a higher rank than presbyters (On Ephesians, ch. 4), or that they are instituted by a different ordination; and he now and then teaches certain other things little in keeping with the common mind of catholics.

Moreover, even if there are many things which seem to favour claiming for this Work the same antiquity as Damasus, there also occur in it other things by which it could be pushed back to a much later age. For, to pass over here the fact that Jerome, in his Ecclesiastical Writers, acknowledges no Latin commentary on the Epistles of Paul except Victorinus's, it is not at all improbable that a great deal was carried over into these books from Augustine, Chrysostom and Jerome; indeed also, which is surely worth noting, from that very commentator whose work, published at the end of Jerome's works, is held by many to be Pelagius's. For since there are not a few places which are covered in the same words in both commentaries, and so there is no doubt that one borrowed from the other, we judge it less probable that Pseudo-Jerome, who is so brief and concise, took some things from Ambrosiaster than the reverse. To this it will further be possible to add that this author proves that Christ the Lord is not Son of God by adoption with no less zeal than if he had written after the error of Felix and Elipandus (On Philippians, ch. 2).

If to these differences of period someone adds a certain discrepancy of diction and opinion on the same matter in the expositions of the different epistles, and also an unevenness in the manner of treatment, now most diffuse, now most compressed, there will perhaps be someone who disputes that all these Commentaries are by the same hand, or at least thinks they should be referred to some compiler of this kind who, in gleaning from various Works, many of which have perished, kept certain marks of the time of each in such a way that he likewise added some of his own age. But however great the difficulty in fixing the antiquity either of the Author or of the Work, the handwritten volumes of these Commentaries, as also the writers by whom they are found cited or excerpted, make it plain that they can by no means be assigned to a time later than the eighth century.

There will perhaps be some who are eager to know our opinion about the Author of the Questions on the New and Old Testament, whom many, following the Louvain theologians, by whom those books were relegated to the appendix of the Works of Saint Augustine (vol. 3, part 1), have judged to be the same as Ambrosiaster. But what we have argued so far shows well enough that deciding this matter is no easy business. Indeed very many things are brought forward which strike the eye in both Works in the same words and with the same passages of Scripture cited; but nothing can be gathered from this except that these very things were copied from one into the other. Yet it is more probable that the author of the Questions, if indeed they have a single author, since he is much more diffuse in treatment and has added several errors of his own to those of Ambrosiaster, was the compiler of the latter.

However, since it cannot be denied that this Work has its usefulness, and since up to this edition it has held a place among the commentaries of Ambrose and is met with here and there cited under his name, we have admitted it into this Appendix all the more gladly because several manuscripts were at hand, with whose help it might come out much more correct. Among other emendations, we have restored a very long fragment at the end of the Commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, and likewise at the beginning of the following one, the loss of which some scribe had patched up from a shred of the Commentary of Pseudo-Jerome.

It remains only to point out that the Commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews has been left out by us. Neither Amerbach nor Erasmus, the older editors, acknowledged it. And when it had been admitted by those who afterwards undertook the care of the Ambrosian edition, it so little deceived men of sharper judgement that it was not even believed to be by the same author to whom the preceding [commentaries] are attributed, much less, then, by our Doctor. And in truth it is nothing else than an ill-arranged compilation from several Fathers, which, since it has been published in fuller form among the Works of Rabanus Maurus, where the authors of the individual fragments can be read alongside, we saw no reason why it should be taken into our edition.
